Extract 1. Questions 19 to 25.
You hear Professor Beth Cartmill giving a presentation on traumatic brain injury to a group of medical professionals.
You now have 90 seconds to read questions 19 to 25.
Thank you.
Thank you.
My name's Beth Cartmill, and I'm a professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation.
I'd like to begin by clarifying what traumatic brain injury actually is.
A TBI, as it's commonly referred to, is when an external physical force leads to a disruption in brain function.
Falls and motor vehicle accidents are the most common causes, but damage also results from many other injuries,
including blast injuries that are frequently experienced by active-duty military personnel.
In 2014, almost 3 million Americans received some type of medical care, or died from a TBI-related incident.
Problems with attention, memory, planning, reasoning, or problem-solving are common,
but often more troublesome are the frequent emotional and behavioural changes.
These changes clearly affect the patient, but it's their resounding impact on loved ones that's so startling.
How a person affected by traumatic brain injury behaves depends on what part or parts of the brain are injured.
The frontal lobe, for example, helps govern personality and impulsivity.
If damaged, there might be no breaking mechanism for self-control, especially in terms of their anger or aggression.
They often make inappropriate comments to friends or strangers, not realizing they're inappropriate.
Others feel they're constantly on an emotional rollercoaster, full of glee and excitement one moment, devastated the next with unpredictable bouts of laughter or sadness without understanding why.
Society sees such behaviour from afar, blind to the individual cause, and this tends to exacerbate feelings of frustration and isolation, fueling such erratic behaviour even further.
Occasionally, the opposite will occur, where the personality may become muted or seemingly emotionless in what's known as flat affect.
Such behaviour can be modified, and rehabilitative care can lead to tremendous breakthroughs, whether this begins immediately following the injury or decades later.
Most people can easily determine when someone is feeling sad or anxious.
This recognition will often trigger the person to offer a comforting gesture
or even have a contagious emotional reaction, causing them to also feel sad or anxious too.
These important actions are referred to as emotion recognition and empathy,
and they are fundamental to creating human emotional connections and relationships.
But imagine when somebody you are close to
suddenly loses the ability to recognize and empathize with your feelings.
For the last couple of decades, researchers have been showing this to be a common outcome for people who have suffered a traumatic brain injury, and one for which they have no control over.
I started studying emotion recognition and empathy in 2005.
At that time, the wife of my first research participant helped put the effects of TBI into perspective for me.
She described her husband loving, caring, and once a very affectionate partner who responded to her emotional needs.
This abruptly changed after what was considered only a minor car crash, turning her husband into someone almost unrecognizable.
He now failed to see her sadness or comfort her during her most desperate times.
Conversely, he was unable to feel the emotional contagion of her happiness when she received recognition at work.
This was indeed quite surprising to me at the time, as it was an aspect of TBI that, until then, I hadn't considered.
Over the years, I've now seen many more such cases with similar patient outcomes.
Treatment options are varied and should always include a multifaceted approach.
Clinicians treating people with TBI should first plan to evaluate emotion recognition and empathy in their patients
and learn how to treat these impairments.
Interviewing patients with TBI and their family members can help paint a picture of how a person has changed,
compared to his or her pre-injury self, and lead to goals for rehabilitation.
Making use of evidence-based approaches is imperative for improving emotion recognition skills,
but no approach should go untested.
We are dealing with individuals, and each case should be treated independently of the other.
When training emotion recognition after TBI, clinicians should also discuss with the patient ways they can respond empathically to loved ones.
Recent research from a group in the Netherlands shows that this combination, both recognition and responding empathically, is highly effective.
Finally, I'd like to mention the impact of good education.
education. Clinicians need to consider educating survivors of TBI and their families about the
common as well as the exceptional changes after TBI. This includes why such changes occur, what
they might expect in terms of behaviour modification, and notifying them that it is indeed possible
to improve with treatment. Family members also should be directed to be more explicit about their
emotions and what they would like from their loved one with a brain injury.
Together, these efforts can improve outcomes after TBI and minimize the common relationship
strains experienced after a brain injury.
